items.title: Background
items.text: Most ligand discovery pipelines treat a target protein as a single rigid structure, typically whatever conformation happens to be available from a crystal structure or a single predicted model. In reality, proteins are dynamic ensembles. They sample multiple conformational substates, some only transiently, and many biologically important recognition events depend on states that are rare, short-lived, or absent from static structural databases. These include allosteric regulation, cryptic pocket opening, order-disorder transitions, and conformational selection in signaling.

items.title: What Lynceus Is
items.text:
Lynceus is a modular computational platform for discovering molecules that recognize specific protein conformational states and couple that recognition to a desired biological outcome.

The central premise is that conformational state is itself the design target, not an afterthought to be handled by post-hoc induced-fit correction.

items.title: Goals
items.text:
• Treat the target as an ensemble. Generate a representative set of target conformational states up front, and screen against that ensemble rather than a single structure.
  • Find sites that only exist in some states. Detect binding sites across all ensemble members, including cryptic and transient pockets, and consolidate them into a distinct set of physical binding sites.
  • Support ultra-large virtual screening out of the box. Train a surrogate model per binding site so that libraries of millions to billions of compounds can be screened against an ensemble of target states, with only a small fraction of the library needing to be docked.
  • Report state preference, not just affinity. Produce candidates (small molecules, proteins, etc.) annotated with the conformational state they favor, which is the information needed to link binding to a functional outcome.
  • Stay modular. Keep each stage (target ensemble generation, binding-site detection, candidate preprocessing and filtering, surrogate training, complex generation) independently replaceable and parallelizable.

items.title: Intended Outcomes
items.text:
Lynceus is designed to support state-selective discovery, such as:

  • Stabilizing an inactive state of a target
  • Blocking an interface that only forms transiently
  • Selectively engaging a disease-associated conformation over the wild-type or resting one

items.title: High-Level Workflow
items.text:
1. Target preparation: Retrieve the target and generate a conformational ensemble.
  2. Binding-site discovery: Detect binding sites on each ensemble member, then deduplicate them into a set of distinct sites, each tracking the members in which it appears.
  3. Candidate preparation: Retrieve, preprocess, repartition, and apply physicochemical filters to the candidate library.
  4. Surrogate modeling (per site): Sample candidates, generate training complexes, and train a surrogate model that predicts binding behavior for that site.
  5. Surrogate filtering (per site): Apply the surrogate to the full filtered library to select promising candidates.
  6. Complex generation (per site): Generate candidate conformers and build complexes against each binding site for downstream analysis.

From the binding-site stage onward, every step runs as an independent fan-out per deduplicated binding site rather than once per run.

items.title: About the Name
items.text: Lynceus is named after the mythological figure renowned for extraordinary vision, reflecting the platform's goal of identifying transient conformations, cryptic interfaces, and the actionable protein states they represent.

items.title: Status
items.text: Lynceus is in early-stage development (alpha). Features and APIs are unstable and subject to breaking changes, and it is not yet suitable for production use.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Lynceus is orchestrated with Argo Workflows running on Kubernetes.

A single run carries one target ensemble. Binding sites are detected on every ensemble member and consolidated into a distinct set of physical binding sites. From that point on, each binding site gets its own independent surrogate model, trained against the shared candidate library.

This page shows how the stages fit together. Candidate preparation and surrogate modeling are covered in detail on their own pages.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Candidates are the compounds screened against each binding site. This page covers how a candidate library is loaded and prepared before it reaches the surrogate model. Lynceus is built to handle libraries of up to roughly a billion compounds, such as ZINC22, so every stage is designed to run in parallel over partitions of the library rather than over the library as a whole.

The output of this stage is a single preprocessed candidate set. It is shared by every binding site and consumed by the surrogate model.

items.title: Workflow
items.text:
flowchart TD
  Source[("Source Library<br>(.smi.gz files)")]

  subgraph Load["Load and Shard"]
    Plan["Plan"]

    Plan --> Batch1["Shard Batch 1"]
    Plan --> Batch2["Shard Batch 2"]
    Plan --> BatchN["Shard Batch N"]

    Batch1 --> Merge["Merge Shards"]
    Batch2 --> Merge
    BatchN --> Merge
  end

  Shards[("Sharded Candidates")]

  subgraph Prep["Preprocess"]
    Shards --> Preprocess1["Preprocess Shard 1"]
    Shards --> Preprocess2["Preprocess Shard 2"]
    Shards --> PreprocessN["Preprocess Shard N"]
  end

  Prepared[("Preprocessed Candidates")]

  Source --> Plan
  Merge --> Shards
  Preprocess1 --> Prepared
  Preprocess2 --> Prepared
  PreprocessN --> Prepared

items.title: Load and shard
items.text:
The source library is supplied as many compressed SMILES files. Loading reads these files in parallel and writes them into a fixed number of hash-partitioned Parquet shards.

  1. Plan: inspect the source files and group them into batches of bounded size, so each batch fits comfortably in a single pod.
  2. Shard: each batch is processed independently, and every compound is assigned to a shard by hashing its identifier. Because the assignment is a pure function of the identifier, shards are uniform in size and a given compound always lands in the same shard.
  3. Merge: the small files written for each shard are consolidated into a single Parquet file per shard.

The result is a library split into a fixed number of evenly sized shards (512 by default), which later stages can process in parallel and from which they can draw representative samples.

items.title: Preprocess
items.text: Each shard is standardized and prepared for downstream use, so that every later stage works from the same consistent representation of the library.

items.title: Outputs
items.text: Output Description Sharded candidates The full library as evenly sized, hash-partitioned Parquet shards Preprocessed candidates The standardized library, shared by all binding sites

items.title: Next steps
items.text: Preprocessed candidates are sampled to train a surrogate model for each binding site, and the trained surrogates are then applied to the full library. See Surrogate Model for details.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Active learning using gradient boosted trees over molecular fingerprint features, trained per binding site.

Fingerprints are computed from the conformers produced during candidate preprocessing. Preprocessing is independent of the binding site, so its computational cost is amortized across every surrogate.

items.title: Workflow
items.text:
flowchart TD

    subgraph FeatureGen ["Feature Generation"]
        Candidates[("Preprocessed<br>Candidates")]
        Candidates -- "fingerprinting" --> Fingerprints[("Molecular<br>Fingerprints")]
    end

    subgraph SeedData ["Seed Data (Round 0)"]
        Fingerprints --> Samples["Samples<br>(uniform)"]
        Samples --> Docking{"Run<br/>docking"}
        Docking --> Labels[("Labels<br>(Affinity)")]
    end

    subgraph ActiveTraining ["Active Training (Round N)"]
        Fingerprints --> TrainSurrogate{"Train<br/>surrogate"}
        Labels --> TrainSurrogate
        TrainSurrogate --> Surrogate[("Surrogate")]

        Surrogate --> PredictLabel{"Predict"}
        Fingerprints --> PredictLabel
        PredictLabel --> Scores["Predicted<br/>Affinity"]

        Scores -- "top-k" --> ActiveSet["Active Set"]
        Fingerprints -- "random sample" --> UniformSet["Uniform Set"]

        ActiveSet --> RoundSamples["Round Samples"]
        UniformSet --> RoundSamples

        RoundSamples --> Docking
    end
